solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Conservative following unpleasant persons’ pathetic tale (3,5)

indicators.note: the Conservative comes after the persons, so TORY is placed last

blocks.note: SOBs, the abbreviation for sons of bitches, i.e. nasty people
a Tory is a member of Britain's Conservative party

annotation.surface: A grumble that some nasty right-wingers have spun a feeble story.
annotation.walkthrough: The possessive in 'persons’' is just surface: SOBS supplies the letters and the apostrophe does no work.
annotation.definitionFit: A sob story is a tale told to win pity, which is exactly a pathetic tale.

entries.clue: Exceptional clue? (6)

blocks.note: first definition: an adjective meaning outstanding, as in a notable success
second definition: a noun meaning a sign, cue or hint

annotation.walkthrough: The adjective sense of signal is the hard half; most solvers only know the noun. The question mark flags that 'clue' is being used as a plain word, not a crossword clue.
annotation.definitionFit: Signal means both notable (adjective) and a sign or hint (noun).

entries.clue: Risk to health — bachelor, one with nothing to say, tentatively? (9)

blocks.note: B = bachelor, as in degree abbreviations
to hazard a guess is to say it tentatively

annotation.surface: A single man who never speaks up is hesitantly described as a danger to health.
annotation.walkthrough: 'One with nothing to say' reads as a silent person, but it splits into I, O and the verb phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: A biohazard is a biological substance that threatens health.

entries.clue: Battels misused for MDMA consignment? (7)

indicators.note: the letters are put to wrong use, i.e. rearranged

annotation.surface: An Oxford student spends the college account on a delivery of ecstasy.
annotation.walkthrough: Battels are the termly accounts an Oxford college bills its students. MDMA is ecstasy, sold as pills, so the question mark marks a definition by example.
annotation.definitionFit: Ecstasy usually comes in tablets, so a consignment of it is a batch of tablets.

entries.clue: Former Kent player always around to save English (5)

indicators.note: EVER turned around reads REVE
the reversed word keeps E safe inside it

blocks.note: ever = always, turned round to REVE

annotation.surface: A retired Kent cricketer is forever holding on to an English place.
annotation.walkthrough: Kent reads as the cricket county, but it is Clark Kent, Superman's alter ego, played on film by the late Christopher Reeve.
annotation.definitionFit: Christopher Reeve played Clark Kent in the Superman films and is now dead, hence former.

entries.clue: Old country manufactured spare parts to accommodate India (6)

indicators.note: the letters of SPARE are made into something new
the rearranged letters house the I

blocks.note: India is I in the NATO alphabet
surface padding: spare parts is the phrase the surface needs

annotation.surface: An ancient nation turned out spare parts to supply India.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Parts' belongs to the surface only; SPARE alone is the fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain historical name: the country called Persia in the West until 1935 is now Iran, so it is an old country in both senses.

entries.clue: See file under B — something pencilled in? (7)

indicators.note: in a down answer, ROW sits below B

blocks.note: a file is a line, a row

annotation.surface: An office instruction: look for the document filed under B, a provisional booking.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pencilled in' suggests a tentative diary entry, but eyebrows are pencilled in with makeup.
annotation.definitionFit: Eyebrows are often drawn or filled in with an eyebrow pencil.

entries.clue: Saint in Lisbon quaffing fifty-five shots (5)

indicators.note: SAO drinks in LV, holding it inside

blocks.note: São is Portuguese for saint, as in São Paulo

annotation.surface: A saint in Lisbon knocks back fifty-five shots of drink.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface's shots are drinks; the definition's are gunfire.
annotation.definitionFit: A salvo is a simultaneous discharge of guns, a volley of shots.

entries.clue: Chant, somehow anguished, hard to be ignored (5,3)

indicators.note: the letters are put together some other way
something ignored is disregarded, so the H is not used

blocks.note: anagram fodder once the H goes
H = hard, as on pencils; removed

annotation.surface: A chant sung in anguish, with the difficult part skipped.
annotation.walkthrough: Remove H from ANGUISHED, then rearrange the remaining eight letters.
annotation.definitionFit: The Agnus Dei ('Lamb of God') is a chant from the Latin Mass.

entries.clue: Idiot keeping in with G&S activities (6-2)

indicators.note: GOON holds IN and GS inside

blocks.note: the two letters without the ampersand

annotation.surface: A fool is keen on Gilbert and Sullivan operettas.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In with' looks like 'friendly with', but IN is a piece and 'with' just adds G&S to it.
annotation.definitionFit: Goings-on are things happening, activities (often suspect ones).

entries.clue: Love in pleasing Bible entry developed for novel (7,2,6)

indicators.note: the O goes in among the fodder
the letters are worked into a new form

blocks.note: love = zero in tennis, O; joins the fodder

annotation.surface: An affectionate, attractive passage from scripture was reworked as fiction.
annotation.walkthrough: Christopher Isherwood's 1939 novel of Weimar Berlin; 16 down gives its author.
annotation.definitionFit: Goodbye to Berlin is Isherwood's novel, the basis of the musical Cabaret (23 across).

entries.clue: Plug connected to earth in top universities (7)

indicators.note: AD plus E is placed inside ACME

blocks.note: the acme is the peak, the top
a plug is a piece of promotion, an ad
E = earth, as on electrical wiring

annotation.surface: A plug is wired to earth inside the best universities.
annotation.walkthrough: The plug and earth suggest wiring, but the plug is publicity.
annotation.definitionFit: Academe is the academic world, the universities collectively.

entries.clue: Sound point preceding two more (7)

indicators.note: N comes before the other two points

blocks.note: two more points: ARROW (a pointer) and S, the south point

annotation.surface: A logical argument lays out one point and then two more.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sound' looks like 'valid' or a noise, but it is a sound in the geographic sense, a strait.
annotation.definitionFit: A sound is a narrow sea channel, and narrows are exactly that.

entries.clue: Endless dread in ship: seamen were in dazed state (3,5)

indicators.note: AWE loses its last letter
dread in ship means the dread is inside the ship, so AW sits within SS

annotation.surface: Sailors aboard a ship were stunned with fear.
annotation.walkthrough: To see stars is what happens after a blow to the head.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone who saw stars was dazed, as after a knock on the head.

entries.clue: French friend beheaded one possessed by Devil (8)

indicators.note: PAL loses its first letter
a soul possessed by the Devil is in his grip, so the I is held inside SATAN

annotation.surface: A French companion lost his head, a soul seized by the Devil.
annotation.walkthrough: 'French friend' suggests a dog (an Alsatian is a German shepherd), but only 'French' defines: an Alsatian comes from Alsace in France.
annotation.definitionFit: An Alsatian is a person from Alsace, a region of France, so French.

entries.clue: Grouse hearts Graves perhaps consumes (5)

indicators.note: what is consumed ends up inside the consumer, so WINE swallows the H

blocks.note: Graves is a Bordeaux wine region; 'perhaps' marks an example

annotation.surface: A game bird's heart is eaten with a glass of Graves.
annotation.walkthrough: Grouse reads as the game bird on a menu, but here it is the verb, to complain.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, in the verb sense: grouse is informal for complain, the bird's name borrowed for grumbling.

entries.clue: Writer is with crowd outside court (9)

indicators.note: a crowd outside a court surrounds it, so HERD wraps round WOO

blocks.note: to court someone is to woo them

annotation.surface: An author stands with a throng outside a law court.
annotation.walkthrough: Court looks like a place; it is the verb, to woo. Christopher Isherwood wrote the novel at 10 across.
annotation.definitionFit: Christopher Isherwood was an English novelist.

entries.clue: Plant elegant parrot devours quietly (8)

indicators.note: what a parrot devours goes inside it, so KEA swallows the P

blocks.note: the kea is a New Zealand parrot

annotation.surface: A smart parrot silently gobbles up a plant.
annotation.walkthrough: The kea is a crossword regular among birds.
annotation.definitionFit: The chickpea is a leguminous plant as well as its seed.

entries.clue: Spirits not initially present: some here perhaps! (5)

definitions.text: Spirits not initially present: some here perhaps!

indicators.note: not present at the start, so the first letter is taken away

blocks.note: shades are ghosts, spirits of the dead; lose the S

annotation.surface: Ghosts are absent at the start, though some may be found here.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: SHADES minus its first letter gives the place where shades dwell.
annotation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Hades is the underworld, home of the shades of the dead.

entries.clue: Loris butchered at home: delicious meat (7)

indicators.note: the letters of LORIS are hacked about

blocks.note: to be in is to be at home

annotation.surface: A slow loris is carved up at home into a tasty joint.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Butchered' fits the meat so snugly it is easy to miss as the anagram signal.
annotation.definitionFit: Sirloin is a prime cut of beef.

entries.clue: Drunk aunt stops woman quaffing black and tan (8)

indicators.note: a drunk aunt is all over the place, so her letters are jumbled
the scrambled letters plug the gap inside SHE
the scrambled AUNT swallows B

annotation.surface: A tipsy aunt blocks a woman drinking a black and tan, the beer-and-stout mix.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Black and tan' is a pub drink, but the split falls after 'black'.
annotation.definitionFit: To tan is to lie in the sun to brown, to sunbathe.

entries.clue: Strong women almost stagger working with spades (7)

indicators.note: AMAZE stops one letter short

blocks.note: AMAZE (to stagger, astonish) without its last letter
a machine that is on is working

annotation.surface: Powerful women nearly totter while digging with spades.
annotation.walkthrough: Stagger here means astonish, not totter.
annotation.definitionFit: Amazons were legendary warrior women; the word now means tall, strong women.

entries.clue: Take furtive look round a new tower at Pisa? (6)

indicators.note: the look goes all round the other letters, so LEER surrounds A and N

blocks.note: to leer is to look slyly

annotation.surface: Sneak a peek at a new tower in Pisa.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark admits a whimsical definition: the Leaning Tower of Pisa is something that leans.
annotation.definitionFit: The Leaning Tower of Pisa leans, so it is jokingly a leaner.

entries.clue: Carriage about to stop at nightclub (7)

indicators.note: RE plugs AT, going inside it

blocks.note: a cab was a horse-drawn carriage for hire
the word as printed, split by RE

annotation.surface: A carriage is about to pull up at a nightclub.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About to' reads as 'going to', but 'about' is RE and 'to stop' is the container instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: A cabaret is a nightclub with floor-show entertainment.

entries.clue: Wooden ships damaged by this tidal wave on river (5)

indicators.note: in a down answer, BORE sits on top of R

blocks.note: a bore is a tidal surge up a river, like the Severn Bore

annotation.surface: Wooden ships wrecked by a tidal wave coming up a river.
annotation.walkthrough: The tidal wave in the surface seems to be the damage; the damage is done by a boring worm or mollusc.
annotation.definitionFit: Shipworms and similar borers drill into wooden hulls, damaging them.

entries.clue: Right character feeding bird in treeless plain (7)

indicators.note: R and AIR are fed into PIE

blocks.note: an air is a manner or character

annotation.surface: The right sort of creature feeds a bird out on the open grassland.
annotation.walkthrough: Pie for magpie is an old word that crosswords keep alive.
annotation.definitionFit: A prairie is a wide, grassy, largely treeless plain.

entries.clue: Musician Philip seen with his missus? (5)

blocks.note: Pip is a nickname for Philip, as in Great Expectations
ER = Elizabeth Regina, the Queen, wife of Prince Philip

annotation.surface: A musician named Philip turns up with his wife.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Seen with' is just the join. The question mark covers Philip's missus being the Queen, ER.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by class: a piper plays bagpipes or pipes, one kind of musician.

entries.clue: He’s one advertisement for sister to hold over (8,7)

indicators.note: the sister holds the over in her arms, so NUN contains O

blocks.note: a personal is a small ad in a newspaper's personal column
a nun is a religious sister

annotation.surface: A man is the sort who places a lonely-hearts ad for a sister to cuddle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'He's one' reads as a man; the definition means the word 'he' is one.
annotation.definitionFit: 'He' is a personal pronoun, the third person singular masculine.

entries.clue: Wife leaving order is notorious (6)

indicators.note: a wife leaving walks out, so the W goes out of WARRANT

blocks.note: a warrant is an official order

annotation.surface: A wife walking out on a court order is a scandal.
annotation.walkthrough: Arrant, meaning downright, survives mainly in 'arrant nonsense' and 'arrant knave'.
annotation.definitionFit: Arrant means utter, out-and-out, as in a notorious rogue.

entries.clue: Immature king has it in for campaigner (8)

indicators.note: to have something is to possess it, so the immature king holds what follows
'has it in' places the it inside, so SA sits within CRUDE

annotation.surface: A childish king bears a grudge against a campaigner.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Has it in for' is an idiom for bearing a grudge, but it splits into 'has it in' plus the link 'for'.
annotation.definitionFit: A crusader campaigns vigorously for a cause.
